name: Reframe nerves as excitement
summary: Instead of trying to calm down before a high-stakes moment, relabel the racing heart as excitement. Arousal stays high but points towards opportunity rather than threat.
how_to_apply: Just before the meeting or turn, tell yourself (silently or aloud) that you are excited and name what you are excited to get across. Do not try to suppress the arousal.
example_line: (to self, before the board item) I'm excited; this is the bit where I get to show them the numbers.
markers: Early-turn stress markers vs. baseline: pitch_median_hz and pitch_drift_st in Tom's first five turns
speaking_rate_wpm spike and fillers_per_100w in the opening minutes
Self-report from Tom (pre-meeting note) needed to confirm the technique was used
common_mistakes: Telling yourself to calm down, which fights the arousal
Treating the label as magic and skipping preparation
drill: Before each of the next five high-stakes meetings, say 'I'm excited about X' once. The coach compares first-five-turn pitch and rate with meetings where you did not.

name: Long-exhale reset
summary: A few breaths with an exhale longer than the inhale lower physiological arousal within a minute or two. It is the fastest legal sedative before a hard conversation.
how_to_apply: Two to five cycles: a full inhale through the nose, a short top-up inhale, then a slow, long exhale through the mouth. Do it in the minute before speaking or while someone else is talking.
example_line: (no line; done silently while the chair introduces the item)
markers: pitch_median_hz in the first substantive turn vs. Tom's calm-1:1 baseline
speaking_rate_wpm and pauses_per_min in the first two minutes of Tom's speech
Audible sighs on the recording are not a problem unless captured mid-sentence
common_mistakes: Holding the breath instead of lengthening the exhale
Doing it so visibly it reads as exasperation
Expecting it to fix poor preparation
drill: Daily for two weeks: five minutes of exhale-focused breathing, then use two cycles before every meeting you chair. Track first-turn pitch against baseline.

sources.where: Balban et al. 2023, cyclic sighing arm
breath as the base of presence

name: Settle your pitch in the first turns
summary: The opening minutes set your rank in a group: people whose pitch climbs early tend to be ranked lower, those who settle lower and steadier gain influence. The aim is your own relaxed level, not an artificially deep one.
how_to_apply: Make your first one or two contributions short and on firm ground, at your relaxed conversational pitch. Breathe out before the first word.
example_line: Morning all. Quick context before we start: we've got two decisions today and I'll take the second.
markers: pitch_drift_st and pitch_median_hz of Tom's first five turns vs. his median for the meeting
uptalk_share in the opening turns
loudness_db relative to others in the same recording
common_mistakes: Pushing the voice down (strain, creak)
Opening with a long, complex point before the voice has settled
Staying silent for 20 minutes, then entering at a high-stakes moment with cold voice
drill: For four weeks, plan a short, easy first line for each group meeting. The coach charts first-five-turn pitch drift week by week.

sources.where: Cheng et al. 2016, early pitch change and emergent rank
Ko et al. 2015, power and voice

name: Let the end of your turn breathe
summary: Confident speakers do not rush to fill the silence after their point or tack on extra clauses. A clean stop followed by a beat of silence signals that you are not afraid of the response.
how_to_apply: When you have made your point, stop, hold a one to two second silence, and let others respond. Resist adding 'so, yeah' or a second version.
example_line: That's my recommendation: hold the price. [pause]
markers: Turn-final trailers ('so yeah', 'anyway', 'if that makes sense') in the transcript
Gap between Tom's last word and the next speaker
Tom re-starting within 1 s of his own stop (negative)
common_mistakes: Filling the silence with a restatement
Ending with a question that dilutes the point
Pausing so long it sounds like lost thread
drill: For a week, end every substantive turn in meetings with a full stop and silence. The coach counts turn-final trailers before and after.

sources.where: Charisma Myth: pausing and not rushing

name: Slow down for the sentence that matters
summary: You do not need to slow down everything; slowing and pausing around the key claim, number or decision makes it register and remember better while the rest can run at normal speed.
how_to_apply: Mark the one sentence per turn that carries the point. Slow it, pause before the key word, and pause after it.
example_line: We'll save [pause] four million [pause] in year one.
markers: speaking_rate_wpm on the key-sentence segment vs. Tom's turn average
long_pauses placed before numerals or decision words
articulation_rate_wpm stable (not slurred) on the key sentence
common_mistakes: Slowing everything until it drags (lower warmth)
Speeding up through the key number because it feels awkward
Pausing mid-phrase in a way that invites interruption
drill: Read a three-paragraph update aloud, slowing only the headline sentence. Record it; the coach compares rate on the headline vs. the rest.

sources.where: MacGregor et al. 2010, pauses before words aid memory
Jobs vs. Zuckerberg rate and phrasing
pace as one of five vocal elements

name: Same voice after the jab
summary: When a comment stings, hold your volume, pitch and pace exactly where they were. A visible jump in any of them is the clearest audible sign that someone got to you.
how_to_apply: On the turn after a provocation, consciously match your previous loudness and rate, start with a short neutral sentence, then answer.
example_line: Fair question. Here's the number.
markers: loudness_db jump vs. Tom's previous three turns
pitch_median_hz rise of more than ~1-2 st
speaking_rate_wpm rise of more than ~15-20% (rubric heuristics)
pitch_sd_st collapse (flat, clipped delivery)
common_mistakes: Going cold and clipped (also a tell)
Sarcasm
Over-correcting into a whisper
drill: With a colleague, rehearse five provocative challenges. Answer each at baseline volume and pace; the coach reads loudness and rate on each reply.

sources.where: Ko et al. 2015: vocal cues of power

name: Let minor errors pass
summary: Correcting every small inaccuracy or slight makes you look anxious about status. Restraint means choosing which points are worth contesting.
how_to_apply: When someone misstates something minor, ask yourself whether it changes the decision. If not, let it go or note it after the meeting.
example_line: (lets 'roughly 10%' stand when the true figure is 9.6%)
markers: Count of Tom's corrective interjections ('just to correct', 'actually it was') in the transcript
interruptions by Tom that add only a correction
common_mistakes: Letting a material error stand to avoid conflict
Correcting with a sigh or edge in the voice
drill: For one week, write down every correction you were tempted to make in meetings and whether it mattered. Make only the ones that did.

sources.where: dominance vs. prestige routes to influence

name: Do not laugh off your own point
summary: Nervous laughter after your own serious statement undercuts it. Laughter that only you produce, with no one joining, usually signals discomfort rather than ease.
how_to_apply: After making a serious point, hold a neutral face and voice. Save laughter for when something is actually funny.
example_line: The pilot failed. [no laugh] Here's what we learned.
markers: Laughter events attributed right after Tom's own turn with no other laughter
Laughter immediately following bad news or a recommendation
common_mistakes: Laughing to soften bad news
Laughing while apologising
drill: The coach lists every Tom-only laugh for two weeks with the line before it. Pick the pattern (e.g. after bad news) and drop it for the following two weeks.

sources.where: Bitterly et al. 2017: failed humour lowers status

name: Own it in one breath, then fix
summary: When something you own went wrong, a short, plain admission followed straight away by the fix reads as strength. Long explanations read as defensiveness.
how_to_apply: One sentence of ownership with 'I', one sentence of what you are doing about it. No preamble, no blame, no third sentence of justification.
example_line: That's on me; I didn't check the supplier terms. I've fixed the contract and we'll have the signed copy Friday.
markers: Transcript: 'that's on me', 'I got that wrong' followed by a next step within two sentences
apologies count low, no repeated apologies
Turn length on ownership turns (short is better)
common_mistakes: Apologising three times
Owning it while blaming circumstances in the same breath
Taking the blame for things that were not yours (over-ownership)
drill: Think of a recent mistake. Write and say the two-sentence version until it comes out in under 15 seconds.

sources.where: Owens & Hekman 2012: admitting mistakes as humble leadership
Tenney et al.: calibration and credibility

name: A deliberate beat before hard answers
summary: A short, visible pause before answering a difficult question can read as thought rather than panic, especially if a crisp answer follows. But long gaps before agreeing to a request can sound reluctant.
how_to_apply: On a hard or important question, pause about one to two seconds, then open with a direct first sentence. On simple requests you are happy to grant, answer promptly.
example_line: [1.5 s pause] No. We shouldn't launch in March, and here's why.
markers: median_response_gap_s on challenge turns vs. other turns
First sentence after the pause: direct answer vs. fillers or restart
Gap before agreeing to a request (>0.6 s can sound reluctant)
common_mistakes: Pausing then rambling (worse than no pause)
Pausing before saying yes to a favour
Pausing every time, making the conversation feel slow
drill: In a mock Q&A, take a full breath before each answer and open with yes, no or a number. The coach checks gaps and first words.

name: Land the full stop
summary: Let pitch fall at the end of a statement so it sounds finished and owned. A rise at the end of a recommendation turns it into a request for approval and invites interruption.
how_to_apply: On recommendations, decisions and introductions, let the last stressed word drop to a low, settled pitch and hold a beat of silence after it.
example_line: We go with option B. [falling, then pause]
markers: final_rise_st < 0 on recommendation and decision turns
uptalk_share on statements (ignore list items and genuine questions)
Others starting to speak right after a rising ending
common_mistakes: Pushing the drop so hard it sounds curt or creaky
Correcting genuine questions into statements
Treating all rises as bad (list items rise naturally)
drill: Read ten recommendation sentences aloud, landing each with a falling pitch and one-beat pause. The coach checks final_rise_st on each.

sources.where: Charisma Myth: lowering intonation at sentence ends

name: Speak from your natural pitch, not a forced low one
summary: Lower voices are associated with leadership perceptions, but later work found pitch predicts electability rather than ability, and forcing the voice down causes strain and creak. The coachable goal is your relaxed, breath-supported pitch that does not climb under pressure.
how_to_apply: Find your relaxed pitch (e.g. say 'mm-hmm' as if agreeing with a friend) and return to it before key turns. Never try to sound deeper than that.
example_line: (said at relaxed pitch) Let me take you through the risks.
markers: pitch_median_hz vs. Tom's relaxed baseline in high-stakes segments (stability, not lowness)
Creak or fry at phrase ends (not currently measured)
pitch_drift_st across the meeting
common_mistakes: Pushing the voice into the throat for gravitas
Monotone as a side-effect of forcing low
Comparing with someone else's voice
drill: Each morning for a week, hum and speak a sentence at relaxed pitch; before key meetings repeat once. The coach tracks pitch stability, not level.

sources.where: Ko et al. 2015: power raised pitch slightly
Love: finding the natural speaking voice

name: Breathe before the sentence, not mid-sentence
summary: Taking a low, full breath before you start a sentence gives the voice support to the end. Running out of breath leads to rushing, trailing off and creaky endings.
how_to_apply: Before a key sentence, breathe low (belly expands, shoulders still), then speak the whole thought on that breath. Shorten sentences if you run out.
example_line: [breath] Three things changed this quarter.
markers: Loudness tailing off at the end of sentences (loudness_db within-turn decline)
Gasps or audible mid-phrase breaths
Creaky voice at phrase ends (when measured)
common_mistakes: High, gasping chest breaths
Breathing so slowly it creates long gaps
Sentences too long for one breath
drill: Read a paragraph aloud taking one low breath per sentence. Repeat daily for a week; listen for sentence endings staying full.

sources.where: Set Your Voice Free: breathing chapter

name: Stress the operative word
summary: In each important sentence, one or two words carry the meaning. Giving them a pitch peak and slight loudness bump makes the point audible without any extra words.
how_to_apply: Before speaking, pick the operative word (often the number, the contrast or the verb) and lift pitch and volume a touch on it.
example_line: This isn't a COST problem. It's a SPEED problem.
markers: pitch_sd_st and loudness_sd_db on persuasive turns vs. baseline
Peaks aligning with contrast words, numbers and decisions
Monotone (low pitch_sd_st) on Tom's key turns
common_mistakes: Stressing every word (no contrast left)
Stressing filler words ('I REALLY think')
Sing-song delivery in a 1:1
drill: Mark one operative word per sentence in a short script and read it twice: flat, then stressed. The coach compares pitch_sd_st.

sources.where: Toastmasters vocal variety: where to place emphasis
animated voice as a charismatic tactic

name: Widen your pitch range when persuading
summary: Speakers rated as more charismatic use more pitch movement. Monotone delivery in a pitch or recommendation reads as low energy or low belief.
how_to_apply: In persuasive turns, let your voice move more than in routine updates: higher on the new or exciting idea, lower on the conclusion.
example_line: Imagine every branch with this in place by spring. That's the prize.
markers: pitch_range_st and pitch_sd_st up vs. Tom's baseline in persuasive turns
A drop of >25% in pitch_sd_st when Tom is making his case (rubric heuristic)
common_mistakes: Performative swoops that sound sales-y
Range collapsing under challenge
Copying a TED cadence in a small meeting
drill: Read a paragraph twice, 'to a friend' and 'to a board'; keep the board version varied but slower. Compare pitch_range_st.

name: Contrast in loudness, not more loudness
summary: Authority comes from varying volume to mark what matters, not from being loud throughout. Greater loudness variability is linked to perceived dominance and power.
how_to_apply: Keep a comfortable base volume and add a small lift on key words; occasionally drop volume to draw people in on a crucial point.
example_line: (quieter) And this is the part I'd ask you to remember.
markers: loudness_sd_db up vs. baseline in persuasive turns
Mean loudness_db relative to others in the same recording (only if Tom is markedly quieter)
common_mistakes: Shouting to hold the floor
Dropping so quiet that remote listeners lose words
Uniform volume throughout
drill: Deliver a two-minute update with one deliberate quiet moment and two lifted key words. The coach checks loudness_sd_db.

sources.where: Ko et al. 2015: loudness variability in high-power speakers

name: Pause before the key word
summary: A short silent pause just before an important word or number makes listeners attend to it and remember it better.
how_to_apply: Place a half to one second silence right before the number, name or decision you want remembered.
example_line: Revenue grew [pause] eleven percent.
markers: long_pauses or pauses_per_min with pauses located before numerals and decision words
Filled pauses ('um') in the same position (negative)
common_mistakes: Pausing before every word
Filling the pause with 'um'
Pauses so long in a competitive group that someone takes the floor
drill: Before any number in your next five meetings, pause one beat. The coach checks pause placement before numerals in the transcript.

sources.where: Conrad et al. 2013: brief frequent pauses

name: Pause after the point to let it land
summary: After a key point, silence gives listeners time to absorb it and signals confidence. Rushing on makes the point feel disposable.
how_to_apply: After a headline, a striking fact or a decision, stop for one to two seconds before moving on.
example_line: We're closing the Leeds site. [2 s] Here's how we'll look after the team.
markers: Silence after headline or decision sentences within Tom's turns
pause_time_s share in presentation turns vs. baseline
common_mistakes: Silence that ends up handing away the floor in a fast group
Pausing after trivial points too
drill: Record a three-minute presentation with a two-second silence after each of your three main points; listen back for impact.

name: Swap fillers for silence
summary: Filled pauses ('um', 'uh', 'you know') make listeners think you know less, and are the strongest single cue to perceived uncertainty. A silent pause does the same planning job without the cost.
how_to_apply: When you feel a filler coming, close your mouth and pause instead. Focus on fillers just before your main claim first.
example_line: The answer is [silence] no.
markers: fillers_per_100w vs. baseline (note ASR under-counts 'um')
Fillers within the 3 words before a claim or number
pauses_per_min rising as fillers fall (expected)
common_mistakes: Aiming for zero (sounds scripted)
Replacing 'um' with 'so' or 'basically'
Speaking faster to avoid pauses
drill: Record a two-minute impromptu answer daily for a week, replacing every 'um' with silence. The coach tracks fillers_per_100w.

name: Finish the sentence you started
summary: False starts and abandoned sentences are part of the 'powerless' style that lowers credibility. Finishing one complete sentence beats starting three.
how_to_apply: If you lose the thread, finish the current sentence simply, pause, then start the next thought cleanly.
example_line: The risk is timing. [pause] Let me explain why.
markers: Restarts and abandoned clauses in the transcript ('So we... the thing is... basically')
Fillers clustered around restarts
common_mistakes: Pressing on with a broken sentence
Starting with long subordinate clauses that cannot be finished
drill: Answer five unexpected questions with a rule: first sentence under 12 words and complete. The coach counts restarts.

sources.where: Get to the Point: complete points

name: Late-night radio voice to calm things down
summary: A slower, lower, softer, downward-inflected voice calms a tense exchange better than telling people to calm down. Voss presents it as his de-escalation register.
how_to_apply: When tension rises, drop your pace and volume a notch and let sentences end downward. Keep it warm, not patronising.
example_line: (slow, low) I can hear this has been a frustrating few weeks.
markers: speaking_rate_wpm and loudness_db falling on Tom's turns as tension rises
Other speaker's loudness and turn length after Tom's turn (de-escalation)
common_mistakes: Sounding condescending or therapeutic
Using it in a routine meeting where it sounds odd
Monotone
drill: Rehearse three tense scenarios with a colleague using the calm register; the coach compares rate and loudness against your normal challenge replies.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference; MasterClass on tone

name: Warm, light default register
summary: For most work conversation, a relaxed, positive tone (smiling in the voice) makes people more cooperative and open than a flat or assertive tone. The assertive register is best kept for rare moments.
how_to_apply: Default to an easy, upbeat tone; let a smile into the voice on greetings and requests. Reserve the clipped, assertive tone for a real line in the sand.
example_line: Morning! Good news first, then one thing I need your help with.
markers: Laughter and back-channels around Tom's turns
pitch_sd_st moderate (not flat) in routine turns
Others' reply speed and length
common_mistakes: Forced cheerfulness in bad-news moments
Never switching to firmness when needed
drill: In the first minute of each 1:1 this week, open with a light, warm line. The coach notes laughter and the other person's first-turn length.

name: Warm up the voice before big meetings
summary: Singers and actors warm up; speakers rarely do. A few minutes of humming, lip trills and sirens makes the first words of the meeting sound like the tenth.
how_to_apply: Five minutes before: hum on a comfortable note, do lip trills sliding up and down, then say your opening line aloud twice.
example_line: (warm-up) Mmm-mmm... brrr... 'Thanks all, two decisions today.'
markers: Pitch and loudness stability in the first two turns vs. later turns
Creak or roughness in the opening turn
common_mistakes: Doing it in an open-plan office where it becomes a distraction
Over-straining the voice
drill: Do a five-minute warm-up before the next three presentations; compare your first-turn pitch and loudness with meetings where you did not.

name: Vary pace with meaning
summary: Pace is a tool: slower for weight, risk and decisions; a little quicker for context and momentum. Studies disagree on whether faster or slower is better overall, which is a reason to vary, not to fix one speed.
how_to_apply: Speed up slightly through background, slow down for the conclusion and any number, and avoid speeding up when challenged.
example_line: (brisk) Quick background on the pilot. (slower) What it tells us is: we should stop.
markers: speaking_rate_wpm by segment within a turn
Rate rise >15-20% on challenge turns (rushing, rubric heuristic)
common_mistakes: One steady rate for everything
Rushing at the end of long turns
Dragging so slowly it sounds condescending
drill: Record a two-minute update in three segments (context, finding, recommendation) at three deliberate speeds. The coach plots rate by segment.

sources.where: Smith et al. 1975 rate; Tusing & Dillard 2000

name: Short phrases, short sentences
summary: Shorter phrases between pauses and shorter sentences are easier to follow, easier to stress and leave fewer chances to stumble. The more charismatic speaker in Niebuhr's comparison used shorter phrases.
how_to_apply: Break long thoughts into short sentences of one idea each. One clause, breathe, next clause.
example_line: Sales are up. Margin is down. That's the problem we need to fix.
markers: Average words per sentence in the transcript
Phrase length between pauses (from pause timestamps)
mean_turn_s alongside sentence length
common_mistakes: Choppy, robotic delivery
Over-simplifying nuanced content
drill: Take one long sentence from last week's transcript and rewrite it as three. Say both versions aloud and record.

name: Watch the creak at phrase ends
summary: Vocal fry (a creaky, low rattle at the end of phrases) often comes from running out of breath. One study found it penalised, but critics say the speakers were imitating fry unnaturally.
how_to_apply: Take a breath before you run out, keep a little air at sentence ends, and avoid pushing pitch below your comfortable floor.
example_line: (sentence ends clean, not crackling) ...and that's why I'd delay.
markers: Creaky phonation at phrase ends (not yet measured by prosody.py)
Octave errors in pitch tracking can signal creak; treat pitch_median_hz drops with care
common_mistakes: Over-correcting into a breathy or pushed voice
Worrying about it more than content
drill: Read a paragraph aloud recording only sentence endings; repeat with a breath before each sentence and compare.

sources.where: Anderson et al. 2014 and Liberman critique

name: Project to the back of the room (or the far microphone)
summary: Presence needs to be heard. Quiet, swallowed speech loses authority in rooms and on calls, and makes people ask you to repeat, which costs momentum.
how_to_apply: Aim your voice at the furthest person (or into the mic at a steady distance). Keep energy to the end of each sentence.
example_line: (projected) Can everyone at the back hear me? Good.
markers: Tom's mean loudness_db vs. other speakers in the same recording (same mic)
Requests to repeat ('sorry, you dropped out')
Loudness decline across a sentence
common_mistakes: Shouting
Leaning away from the mic on calls
Projection that becomes broadcasting (third circle)
drill: In an empty room, speak a paragraph to the far wall without shouting; then do it to a phone recording from across the room and check every word is clear.

name: Bottom line up front
summary: Put the conclusion, recommendation or answer in the first sentence, then the reasons, then detail. A busy listener can stop at any point and still have the point.
how_to_apply: Start substantive turns with 'My recommendation is', 'The answer is' or 'In short'. Context comes after, and only if needed.
example_line: My recommendation is we delay two weeks. Two reasons: payments aren't tested and the contract isn't signed.
markers: Position of the first claim or recommendation phrase in substantive turns (target: within ~25 words)
certainty_per_100w in turn openings
Others asking 'so what are you proposing?' (negative)
common_mistakes: Chronological storytelling before the point
Leading with caveats
Answering first then undoing it with ten qualifications
drill: Before each update this week, write one sentence starting 'I recommend' or 'The answer is' and say it first. The coach checks claim position.

sources.where: Pyramid Principle: start with the answer
Simply Said: lead with the message

name: The 'I believe that' test
summary: A topic is a subject area; a point is a claim someone could disagree with. If your opening cannot follow 'I believe that...', you have a topic, not a point.
how_to_apply: Before speaking, finish the sentence 'I believe that...' and use the completion as your opening line.
example_line: (not 'Let's talk about hiring') We should pause hiring until the March numbers are in.
markers: Turn openings that name a subject ('on pricing', 'about the roadmap') without a claim
Presence of a contestable claim in the first two sentences
common_mistakes: Points so hedged they become topics again
Multiple competing points in one turn
drill: Take the agenda of your next meeting and turn each item into an 'I believe that' sentence before you go in.

sources.where: Get to the Point: point vs. topic, 'I believe that' test

name: Point, reason, example, point
summary: A simple four-beat structure for a contribution: state the point, give the main reason, give one concrete example, restate the point. It keeps impromptu contributions short and complete.
how_to_apply: Use PREP for any contribution longer than a sentence or two; aim for under a minute.
example_line: We should keep the London office. It's where our clients are. Last month three of five new deals came from walk-in meetings. So London stays.
markers: Restatement of the opening claim at the end of the turn
A concrete example (number, name, event) inside the turn
Turn length 30-60 s for contributions
common_mistakes: Three examples instead of one
Skipping the closing restatement
Using it robotically in casual chat
drill: Answer five practice questions with PREP aloud, each under 45 seconds. The coach checks the four beats.

name: Situation, complication, question, answer
summary: For topics that need context, a short opener names the situation everyone agrees on, the complication that changed it, the question this raises, and then your answer. It keeps context brief and purposeful.
how_to_apply: Spend one sentence each on situation, complication and implied question, then give your answer and support.
example_line: We planned to launch in March. The supplier has slipped six weeks. So: launch late or launch thin? I'd launch thin.
markers: Context portion of a turn kept to two or three sentences before the answer
Explicit answer following the complication
common_mistakes: Letting the situation part grow into a history lesson
Omitting the answer
drill: Rewrite your next status update as four lines (S, C, Q, A) and say it in under 40 seconds.

name: Announce the number of points
summary: Telling listeners how many points are coming ('three reasons') gives them a map, signals preparation and makes it easier to hold the floor until you finish.
how_to_apply: Say the number before the list, then label each one ('first', 'second'). Keep it to two or three.
example_line: Two risks. First, supplier lead time. Second, the contract.
markers: Signpost phrases ('two things', 'first', 'second', 'finally') in the transcript
Announced count matching delivered count
common_mistakes: Announcing three and delivering five
Forgetting the third mid-way
Signposting trivial remarks
drill: In every substantive turn this week, announce a count before listing. The coach checks announced vs. delivered counts.

name: Distinct reasons that cover the case
summary: Supporting points should not overlap and together should cover what the listener needs. Overlapping reasons sound like padding; gaps invite the obvious challenge.
how_to_apply: Before a key meeting, list your reasons and check: does any repeat another? Is there an obvious category missing (cost, risk, people, time)?
example_line: Three reasons: it's cheaper, it's faster, and it's lower risk.
markers: Repeated reasons in different words within one turn
Others raising an obvious category Tom omitted
common_mistakes: Over-engineering structure in casual conversation
Forcing a four-box framework onto everything
drill: Take last week's main recommendation and sort its reasons into non-overlapping groups. Cut the duplicates.

name: What? So what? Now what?
summary: A three-part structure for impromptu contributions: what is happening, why it matters, what we should do next. Useful when asked for a view without warning.
how_to_apply: When called on, organise your reply into the three beats, one or two sentences each.
example_line: Churn rose to 4%. That's two months of growth gone. I'd like us to call the top twenty accounts this week.
markers: Presence of an implication ('which means') and a next step in impromptu turns
Length of impromptu turns (under ~60 s)
common_mistakes: Skipping the 'so what' and going straight to action
Using it for questions that need a yes or no
drill: Ask a colleague for five random workplace questions; answer each with What/So what/Now what in under 45 seconds.

sources.where: Think Faster, Talk Smarter: What-So What-Now What

name: Problem, solution, benefit
summary: For proposals: name the problem, propose the solution, state the benefit. It moves a listener from concern to action in three beats.
how_to_apply: Frame proposals as a problem the listener recognises, your fix, and what they get.
example_line: Approvals take nine days. If we delegate sign-off under £10k, it'll be two. Your team gets a week back on every deal.
markers: Proposal turns containing all three parts
Benefit stated in the listener's terms
common_mistakes: Overstating the problem to sell the solution
Benefits that matter to Tom, not the listener
drill: Draft your next proposal in three sentences using the pattern and rehearse it aloud.

name: Make abstractions concrete
summary: Concrete language (specific numbers, names, objects, examples) is easier to understand, more memorable and makes listeners feel heard. Abstract corporate language feels evasive.
how_to_apply: For every abstract claim, add one concrete anchor: a number, a person, a place or a picture.
example_line: (not 'improve engagement') Get each branch manager opening the dashboard before 9am.
markers: Numerals, named people and concrete nouns per substantive turn
Jargon phrases ('drive synergies', 'going forward', 'leverage')
common_mistakes: Drowning listeners in numbers
Anecdotes that are concrete but irrelevant
drill: The coach picks three abstract sentences from last week's transcript; rewrite each with a number, a person or an image.

sources.where: Bezos Blueprint: plain language and analogies

name: Plain words and no weasel words
summary: Simple words and short sentences make you sound clearer and more confident. Vague softeners ('sort of', 'kind of', 'basically') and passive voice blur ownership.
how_to_apply: Choose the plain word, use active voice ('we missed the date', not 'the date was missed'), and remove vague softeners.
example_line: We missed the date because we underestimated testing.
markers: hedges_per_100w (note 'sort of' / 'kind of' counted there)
Passive constructions on accountability statements
Jargon density
common_mistakes: Over-simplifying technical content for an expert audience
Sounding blunt to the point of rudeness
drill: Edit a page of your own notes to an easy reading level, then present from the edited version.

sources.where: Bezos Blueprint: plain writing, weasel words, active voice

name: Close by restating the headline
summary: End a contribution or presentation by returning to the main point in a single sentence. Listeners remember beginnings and ends; a trailing ending wastes the strongest position.
how_to_apply: Finish substantive turns with 'So, ...' plus your headline, then stop.
example_line: So: delay two weeks, and we launch clean.
markers: Final sentence of a turn matching the opening claim
Turn-final trailers ('anyway', 'so yeah', 'I don't know')
common_mistakes: Adding new information in the close
Summarising at length
drill: For each turn longer than 30 seconds this week, end with a 'So,' sentence. The coach checks the last sentence of long turns.

name: Build from what they already know
summary: New ideas land when they are built step by step from concepts the audience already has. Starting from the listener's existing model keeps you from losing them.
how_to_apply: Identify one concept the audience already holds and anchor your explanation to it before adding the new piece.
example_line: You know how we price consulting by day rate. This works the same, except the 'day' is a data feed.
markers: Explanations that reference the listener's known context
Clarifying questions from others after Tom's explanations (fewer is better)
common_mistakes: Patronising experts
Taking too long building the base
drill: Explain a complex part of your strategy to a non-specialist in two minutes, starting from something they already know.

sources.where: TED Talks: building the idea from familiar concepts
Resonate: start where the audience is

name: Signal the transitions
summary: Short transition lines ('That's the cost side; now the risk') tell listeners where they are. They make long contributions feel organised and make it harder to be interrupted mid-structure.
how_to_apply: When moving between parts, say where you've been and where you're going in one short sentence.
example_line: That's why it's affordable. Now, why it's safe.
markers: Transition phrases in turns longer than ~60 s
Interruptions of Tom mid-structure (fewer is better)
common_mistakes: Over-signposting short answers
Transitions that repeat the whole previous section
drill: Present a three-part update and record it; check that each part is introduced with a one-line transition.

name: Know, feel, do: define your intent first
summary: Before any important communication, decide what you want the listener to know, feel and do afterwards. Without that, people over-explain and drift.
how_to_apply: Write the three lines before the meeting; open with the 'do' if it is a request, with the 'know' if it is an update.
example_line: (prep note) Know: we're behind. Feel: confident we'll recover. Do: approve two contractors.
markers: Whether the 'do' (ask) appears explicitly in the transcript
Drift: proportion of turn time on topics outside the stated intent
common_mistakes: Defining the intent but never stating the ask
Too many intents in one meeting
drill: Before the next three key meetings, write know/feel/do. The coach checks whether the 'do' was said aloud.

sources.where: Power of Presence: intention and feeling

name: Cut diffuse hedges from recommendations
summary: Stacked hedges ('I sort of think maybe') lower credibility and persuasion. In recommendation and decision turns, say what you think.
how_to_apply: In recommendation turns, delete 'just', 'sort of', 'maybe', 'I guess', 'a bit'. Keep at most one precise qualifier, after the claim.
example_line: (not 'I guess maybe B?') I'd back option B.
markers: hedges_per_100w in recommendation turns vs. baseline
certainty_per_100w in decision moments
British politeness forms in routine turns should not be over-penalised
common_mistakes: Removing all softening and sounding brusque with UK colleagues
Replacing hedges with false certainty
drill: The coach lists your top five hedge phrases each week; pick one to drop in recommendation turns for the next week.

name: Commit, then qualify once
summary: State your position first, then the single most important uncertainty and how you will handle it. Committed and calibrated beats both diffuse hedging and blanket certainty.
how_to_apply: Use the pattern: 'I recommend X. The main risk is Y; here's how we'd handle it.' One qualifier, after the commitment.
example_line: I'd go with B. The risk I can't size yet is lead time; I'll have it Friday.
markers: Recommendation phrase preceding the qualifier in the same turn
Count of qualifiers per recommendation (one is ideal)
common_mistakes: Qualifying before committing
Listing every conceivable risk
No qualifier on a genuinely uncertain call
drill: Practise five recommendations aloud using the commit-then-qualify pattern; the coach checks order in the transcript.

sources.where: Tenney et al.: calibration trumps confidence

name: Put a number on your confidence
summary: People do not dislike uncertain advice when it is expressed precisely (ranges, probabilities, 'more likely than'). Vague 'I'm not sure' is what costs credibility.
how_to_apply: Replace 'I'm not sure' with a likelihood, range or comparison: '70%', 'between 3 and 5 weeks', 'more likely than not'.
example_line: I'd put it at 70% we hit March; the range is three to five weeks late if we don't.
markers: Numeric probabilities, ranges or comparative likelihood phrases (positive)
'I'm not sure / no idea' without a range (negative)
common_mistakes: False precision on things you have no basis to estimate
Using numbers to avoid committing to a recommendation
drill: For a week, every time you would say 'not sure', give a percentage or range instead. The coach counts calibrated phrases.

sources.where: Gaertig & Simmons 2018: uncertain advice not disliked when precise

name: Say what would change your mind
summary: Naming the evidence that would change your view shows confidence and openness at once. It reads as conviction held for reasons, not ego.
how_to_apply: After stating a position on a contested topic, add one line: 'What would change my mind is...'
example_line: I'd keep the price. What would change my mind is if churn tops 5% next month.
markers: 'What would change my mind' / 'if X, I'd rethink' phrases
Other speakers responding with evidence rather than opposition
common_mistakes: Naming a condition that could never be met
Using it so often it sounds unsure
drill: In the next two debates, add a 'change my mind' line after your position.

name: Drop the permission tags
summary: Tags like 'does that make sense?', 'is that OK?' or 'right?' after a recommendation turn it into a request for approval. Tag questions lower perceived power and credibility.
how_to_apply: End recommendations with a full stop. If you want input, ask a real question: 'What would you push back on?'
example_line: (not 'We delay, if that's OK?') We delay. What would you push back on?
markers: Tags at the end of recommendation turns ('make sense?', 'if that's OK', 'right?')
uptalk_share and final_rise_st on those turns
common_mistakes: Removing all invitations to respond
Replacing tags with an aggressive 'any objections?'
drill: The coach lists every tag after a recommendation for one week. Replace each with a full stop or a genuine open question.

sources.where: Hosman & Siltanen: tag questions and perceived power

name: Contribute without apologising
summary: Opening with 'sorry, can I just...' or 'this might be a silly question' frames your contribution as an imposition and lowers its weight before you start.
how_to_apply: Start with the content. If you need to break in, use the other person's name and a bridge ('Sam, building on that...').
example_line: (not 'Sorry, quick thing, might be stupid') One question on the numbers.
markers: apologies count, especially at turn openings
Minimisers ('just', 'quick', 'silly', 'probably wrong but') in the first five words
common_mistakes: Cutting genuine apologies when you did err
Becoming brusque when interrupting
drill: For one week, no 'sorry' to open a contribution. The coach counts turn-opening apologies.

name: Use 'I' for judgements and decisions
summary: Presence includes owning your view. 'People are saying' or 'it was felt that' hides the judgement; 'I recommend' or 'my view is' owns it. Keep 'we' for shared work.
how_to_apply: When giving a judgement, use first person singular; when describing team work, use 'we'.
example_line: My view is we're not ready. The team has done great work; I'm the one saying wait.
markers: 'I recommend / my view / I've decided' in decision turns
Passive or third-party attributions in place of a view ('it's been suggested')
common_mistakes: 'I' for team achievements
Hiding behind 'we' when delivering bad news you decided
drill: Review three past recommendations; rewrite each opening line in first person, and use that form next time.

name: Give a verdict at the decision point
summary: When the room needs a position, give one: yes, no, or not yet with a date. Executives name decisiveness as a core gravitas trait; dithering at decision points costs more than an imperfect call.
how_to_apply: When asked for a decision, open with the verdict word, then the reason. If you need more data, say exactly what and by when.
example_line: Not yet. I need the legal view, and I'll decide by Thursday.
markers: Direct verdict word (yes/no/not yet/I'd do X) in the first sentence of decision turns
Others asking 'so is that a yes?' (negative)
common_mistakes: Deciding things that are not yours to decide (Leadership coach territory)
Faux-decisiveness without information
drill: In the next five decision moments, open with a verdict word. The coach checks first words.

sources.where: 2022 survey: confidence and decisiveness remain top

name: Do not overclaim
summary: Confidence attracts trust at first, but confident sources who turn out to be wrong lose more credibility than cautious ones. Certainty should match your evidence.
how_to_apply: Match your words to your evidence: 'I know' for facts you have checked, 'I expect' for forecasts, 'I suspect' for hunches.
example_line: I know we lost the Hartley account. I suspect pricing was part of it.
markers: Certainty words ('definitely', 'guaranteed', 'always') attached to forecasts
Later recordings where those forecasts are revisited
common_mistakes: Overcorrecting into constant hedging
Hiding behind 'I suspect' to avoid commitment
drill: For one week, tag each claim you make in meetings as know/expect/suspect in your notes afterwards and check your wording matched.

name: Express confidence you actually have
summary: Listeners prefer advisors who sound confident, often even when they are overconfident. If you are confident, sound it; under-signalling real confidence leaves influence on the table.
how_to_apply: When you are sure, say so plainly and once: 'I'm confident about this because...'
example_line: I'm confident on this one: we've run it in three markets and it held each time.
markers: certainty_per_100w on topics where Tom has strong evidence
Hedges attached to well-evidenced claims (mismatch)
common_mistakes: Using the heuristic to mask weak evidence (see 'Do not overclaim')
Stacking intensifiers ('really, really sure')
drill: Pick the three topics where you have the strongest evidence; prepare one confident sentence for each and use it when they come up.

name: Translate British understatement on serious points
summary: Understatement ('not ideal', 'a bit behind') is normal in UK business but can hide the severity of an issue, especially for international or direct-culture listeners. On serious points, say the plain version.
how_to_apply: When the issue is serious, state its size plainly, then soften the delivery if needed with tone rather than words.
example_line: (not 'it's a bit behind') It's six weeks late and that puts the contract at risk.
markers: Downgraders ('a bit', 'slightly', 'not ideal', 'quite') attached to serious issues
Follow-up questions from others seeking the real size of the problem
common_mistakes: Abandoning politeness entirely with UK colleagues
Over-dramatising
drill: Take three understated lines from recent transcripts and rewrite them with the plain severity; use that phrasing in the next international call.

name: Hold your position under first pushback
summary: Folding at the first challenge signals that the view was not really held. Restate your position with reasons unless you hear a new fact or argument.
how_to_apply: When challenged, ask yourself: is this new information? If not, acknowledge and restate. If yes, say so and update openly.
example_line: I hear the concern. Nothing in it changes the numbers, so I'd still go ahead.
markers: Position reversals within one exchange without new information in the challenger's turn
Restatement phrases after challenge
common_mistakes: Stubbornness in the face of a genuinely new fact
Restating louder rather than clearer
drill: In a practice debate, hold your view through two challenges without new facts, then update when a new fact is introduced.

name: Strategic modesty when your expertise is known
summary: One study found that established experts who expressed some uncertainty were more persuasive (surprise draws attention), but a large 2024 replication did not support this and found certainty helped regardless. Treat as an experiment, not a rule.
how_to_apply: Where everyone already knows you are the expert, you might try opening with a measured, less-than-certain framing and see how it lands.
example_line: I've done twenty of these and I'm still only 70% sure on this one. Here's why.
markers: Calibrated phrases from Tom on his core expertise topics
Others' engagement (questions, turn length) after such openings
common_mistakes: Using modesty on topics where you are not seen as expert
Expressing doubt you do not feel
drill: Try it in two expert contexts and compare engagement with two where you open confidently. Report as personal data only.

sources.where: Karmarkar & Tormala 2010; Løhre et al. 2024 replication

name: A short story with a point
summary: A brief anecdote with a person, a moment and a point is more persuasive than an abstract claim: listeners get absorbed and notice fewer weak points. Stories are among the charismatic tactics that raise leadership ratings.
how_to_apply: Tell 30-60 second stories: who, what happened at a specific moment, and the one-line point. Lead into the point you are making, not away from it.
example_line: Last week a branch manager in Leeds opened the tool three times before nine. That's the bar: daily and useful.
markers: Past-tense narrative segments with a named person or place
A point sentence following the story
Others referring back to the story later
common_mistakes: Stories with no point
Long setups
Stories where Tom is always the hero
drill: Build a bank of five 45-second work stories, each tagged with the point it makes. Use one in a meeting each week.

sources.where: Charismatic Leadership Tactics: stories and anecdotes

name: One fresh image for the core idea
summary: A metaphor or analogy makes an abstract idea concrete and memorable. It is the charismatic tactic most often adopted by others, which spreads your framing.
how_to_apply: For each main idea, find one image from everyday life. Use it early and repeat it once.
example_line: This migration is a bridge, not a destination: we cross it and keep going.
markers: 'It's like / think of it as / imagine' phrases
Others reusing Tom's image later in the meeting (strong positive)
common_mistakes: Mixed or tired metaphors ('move the needle')
Metaphors that need explaining
Too many images competing
drill: Rewrite your current strategic message using one metaphor; test it on two colleagues and keep the one they repeat back.

sources.where: Tur et al. 2022: verbal charisma in TED

name: Not this, but that
summary: Contrasts ('not a cost problem, a speed problem') sharpen the point by showing what it is not. They are among the most effective charismatic tactics and give the voice a natural place to stress.
how_to_apply: Frame your main point as a contrast with the obvious or old view, and stress the contrasting words.
example_line: We're not selling software. We're selling time back.
markers: 'Not X but Y', 'we used to... now...' structures
pitch and loudness peaks on contrasted words (loudness_sd_db, pitch_sd_st)
common_mistakes: Straw-manning colleagues' views
Every sentence a contrast (sounds like slogans)
drill: Turn your next headline into a not-X-but-Y line and deliver it with stress on X and Y.

sources.where: Resonate: contrast between what is and what could be

name: Lists of three
summary: Three-part lists feel complete, are easy to remember, and are one of the verbal charismatic tactics. Two feels thin, four feels like a list.
how_to_apply: Group supporting points, benefits or actions in threes when it is natural; build to the most important.
example_line: It's faster, it's cheaper, and it's safer.
markers: Three-item lists in the transcript
Rising emphasis on the third item
common_mistakes: Forcing a third item that is weak
Overuse until it sounds like a speech
drill: In the next presentation, use one deliberate three-part list per main section and check the third item is the strongest.

sources.where: Talk Like TED: rule of three

name: Ask the question, then answer it
summary: A rhetorical question creates a gap the audience wants filled; answering it yourself delivers the point with momentum.
how_to_apply: Pose the question your audience is silently asking, pause briefly, then answer it.
example_line: So why haven't competitors done this? [pause] Because it only works at our scale.
markers: Question followed by Tom's own answer within the same turn
Short pause between question and answer
common_mistakes: Asking questions you then do not answer
Using it in a 1:1 where it feels like lecturing
drill: Put one rhetorical question into your next update at the point where people usually push back.

name: Reflect the room's sentiment
summary: Naming what the group is feeling ('I know everyone's tired of re-planning') shows you understand them, which is one of the verbal charismatic tactics and earns permission for what you say next.
how_to_apply: Before a demanding message, put the group's likely feeling into one sentence, accurately and without exaggeration.
example_line: I know this is the third plan this year and people are tired of it.
markers: Sentiment-reflecting statements ('I know...', 'you're probably feeling...') before asks
Back-channels or agreement after them
common_mistakes: Projecting feelings people do not have
Using it as a manipulative softener
drill: Before your next team-wide message, write one line naming the group's feeling and test it with a colleague for accuracy.

name: High bar plus belief they can meet it
summary: Setting a demanding expectation and in the same breath expressing confidence that people can meet it is a charismatic tactic. Either half alone is weaker.
how_to_apply: Pair the stretch goal with a specific reason you believe it is achievable.
example_line: This is a hard target, and I've watched this team land two harder ones.
markers: Expectation statement followed by a confidence statement with evidence
common_mistakes: Empty cheerleading
High bar with no reason to believe
This is about voicing it, not setting the goal (Leadership coach)
drill: Rewrite your next target announcement so it contains both a stretch and one concrete reason for confidence.

sources.where: CLTs: high expectations and confidence they can be met

name: Moral conviction, sparingly
summary: Expressing why something is right, not just efficient, is part of charismatic signalling. Overused or used in routine operational talk, it sounds inflated.
how_to_apply: Reserve values language for decisions that really carry it; say it once, plainly.
example_line: We owe our clients the truth on this, even though it costs us the renewal.
markers: Values phrases ('the right thing', 'we owe') in the transcript, and their context
Frequency per meeting (rare is right)
common_mistakes: Moralising about trivial decisions
Values talk not matched by the decision
drill: Identify the one decision this month that truly carries a values dimension and prepare one sentence about it.

name: Contrast what is with what could be
summary: Persuasive presentations alternate between the current reality and the better future, then end on the new future. The gap creates tension the audience wants resolved.
how_to_apply: Structure a pitch or vision talk as alternating beats of 'today...' and 'imagine instead...', ending on the future and the call to action.
example_line: Today, a quote takes nine days. Imagine it taking nine minutes.
markers: Alternating present/future framing in presentation turns
Final section focused on future state and call to action
common_mistakes: All vision, no reality (sounds naive)
All problem, no future (sounds negative)
drill: Storyboard your next pitch as four what-is/what-could-be beats and an ending; rehearse it aloud once.

sources.where: Resonate: sparkline of what is vs. what could be

name: Engineer one memorable line
summary: Plan one moment people will remember and repeat: a crisp phrase, a striking number or a vivid image. Repeat it at the start and end.
how_to_apply: Craft a short, repeatable line for your main point; say it early, use it again to close.
example_line: Boring in the best way: that's the product.
markers: Recurrence of the same phrase in Tom's speech
Others quoting the phrase later (strong positive)
common_mistakes: Gimmicks that overshadow the substance
A line that sounds rehearsed in a small meeting
drill: For your next presentation, write five candidate lines, test them on a colleague, keep the one they remember an hour later.

name: Teach them something new
summary: Audiences pay attention to novelty: an unexpected fact, a counter-intuitive finding or a new way of seeing a familiar problem.
how_to_apply: Lead with the one thing your audience probably does not know yet and that changes how they see the issue.
example_line: Most of our churn isn't price. Two-thirds of leavers never logged in after week one.
markers: Novel facts or findings early in presentation turns
Questions from others asking for more detail (engagement)
common_mistakes: Novelty for its own sake
Surprising claims you cannot back
drill: Before your next update, find one fact the audience doesn't know and open with it.

sources.where: Talk Like TED: teach something new

name: Sensory, specific detail
summary: A few specific sensory details (what someone said, the time, the place) make a story vivid. Generic summaries do not transport listeners.
how_to_apply: In stories, include one specific detail: a time, a place, a short paraphrase of what someone said.
example_line: It was 7am, the car park was empty, and the only light on was the night team's.
markers: Specific times, places and named people in narrative segments
common_mistakes: Over-describing
Details that identify private individuals inappropriately
drill: Rewrite one of your stock stories with three specific details and tell it aloud.

name: Self-deprecate the trivial, never the core
summary: Light self-deprecation about small things (tech, coffee, handwriting) shows ease and warmth. Self-deprecation about your core competence undermines the very trust the room relies on.
how_to_apply: Keep self-deprecating humour to non-essential traits, and keep it short.
example_line: That's the last time I do maths before coffee. Correct figure is 11%.
markers: Laughter events after Tom's turn (laughter with others vs. Tom alone)
Self-deprecating content about strategy, numbers or judgement (negative)
common_mistakes: 'I'm hopeless with numbers' from a strategy lead
Repeated self-deprecation that becomes a pattern
drill: Each week the coach lists Tom's self-deprecating lines; check none touched core competence.

sources.where: Bitterly et al. 2017: humour and status

name: Light humour to signal ease
summary: Successful humour raises perceived confidence and competence; failed or inappropriate humour signals confidence but lowers perceived competence. Low-risk, situational humour is the safest form.
how_to_apply: Use gentle humour about the shared situation, mainly early in meetings or after tension resolves; avoid it during someone's serious concern.
example_line: Third reschedule this month. I'm starting to take it personally.
markers: Laughter events by others after Tom's lines
Humour during challenges (possible deflection)
common_mistakes: Jokes at a junior colleague's expense
Banter in cross-cultural or very senior rooms
Humour to dodge a hard question
drill: Review a month of laughter events with the coach: which lines landed and in what context; repeat the pattern that worked.

name: Let them hear why you care
summary: Audiences respond to speakers who visibly care about their subject. Briefly saying why something matters to you personally adds energy and credibility.
how_to_apply: In a pitch or big update, include one sentence on why this matters to you, then return to them.
example_line: I've wanted to fix this since my first week here: I watched a client wait a month for an answer.
markers: Personal-relevance statements in presentation turns
pitch_sd_st and loudness_sd_db rising on those sentences (animation)
common_mistakes: Making it about you for too long
Faking passion
drill: Write one 'why I care' sentence for your current biggest initiative and use it in the next relevant meeting.

sources.where: Talk Like TED: unleash the master within

name: Connect, then lead
summary: People judge warmth (can I trust you?) before competence (can you deliver?). Leading with warmth and then showing strength gets strength accepted rather than resisted.
how_to_apply: Open conversations with a moment of genuine connection or acknowledgement, then move to substance and direction.
example_line: Thanks for jumping on at short notice; I know it's month-end. Here's what I need us to decide.
markers: First 30-60 s of Tom-led conversations: acknowledgement, names, rapport
Others' first-turn length and tone
common_mistakes: Small talk that drags
Warmth with no strength (sounds like a peer, not a leader)
Strength with no warmth (respected, avoided)
drill: For a week, open each 1:1 and meeting you lead with one genuine acknowledgement line before the agenda.

sources.where: Fiske, Cuddy & Glick 2007: warmth and competence

name: 'We' for shared work, 'I' for decisions
summary: Collective pronouns signal you speak for the group; leaders who win elections use them more. But 'I' remains right for owning decisions and mistakes.
how_to_apply: Use 'we/us/our' for goals and shared work; keep 'I' for judgements, commitments and apologies.
example_line: We've got a hard quarter. I'll take the client conversation; we'll share the rest.
markers: We-ratio (we/us/our vs. I/me/my) vs. baseline in group and vision contexts
'I' on decisions and apologies (positive)
common_mistakes: Royal 'we' that hides accountability
'We' while assigning all work to others
drill: The coach shows three 'I/my' sentences about shared work from last week; rewrite them as 'we'.

name: Name and credit specifics
summary: Crediting a named colleague for a specific contribution signals security and generosity, a core humble-leadership behaviour. Generic thanks does far less.
how_to_apply: Once per meeting, credit someone by name for something specific they did or said.
example_line: Priya's churn analysis is the reason we caught this early.
markers: Name + specific contribution phrases in the transcript
Credit given in the presence of senior people (stronger)
common_mistakes: Generic 'great work everyone'
Credit as a prelude to criticism
Over-crediting that sounds performative
drill: In every meeting this week, name and credit one specific contribution. The coach counts them.

name: Label what they seem to feel
summary: Naming the other person's likely emotion or concern ('it sounds like this has been frustrating') shows you understand and tends to defuse it. It is the core of Voss's tactical empathy.
how_to_apply: Use 'It sounds like / seems like / looks like...' followed by the emotion or concern, then stop and let them respond.
example_line: It sounds like the timeline was set without your team's input.
markers: Labels starting 'it sounds/seems/looks like' in the transcript
Other speaker's next turn: longer and calmer, or 'exactly' (positive)
common_mistakes: Labelling with 'I hear you're...' (focus on self)
Getting the emotion wrong and pressing on
Using labels mechanically
drill: In the next three difficult 1:1s, use at least one label and wait silently for the response.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference: labelling, tactical empathy

name: Single-task attention
summary: Presence in Cabane's sense is giving full attention to the person in front of you; people sense split attention quickly, even on calls.
how_to_apply: Close other windows, put the phone away, and keep your attention on what the person is saying rather than on your next point.
example_line: You said the pilot stalled in week three. What happened that week?
markers: Replies that reference the other person's specific words
'Sorry, could you repeat that?' moments (negative)
Response latency spikes that suggest distraction
common_mistakes: Pretend attention (nodding while rehearsing)
Multitasking on video calls
drill: In five 1:1s this week, ask at least one question that uses the other person's exact words. The coach checks.

name: Second-circle energy
summary: Rodenburg describes three states: withdrawn (first circle), broadcasting at people (third circle), and connected two-way exchange (second circle). Presence lives in the second, with flexibility to use the others deliberately.
how_to_apply: Notice when you are withdrawing (looking down, quiet, waiting) or broadcasting (talking at the room, not reading it), and return to focused exchange with specific people.
example_line: (to one person, not the room) Mark, how does that land for your team?
markers: First circle: low talk_share, quiet loudness_db, short hedged turns
Third circle: high talk_share, long monologues (longest_turn_s), few questions
Second circle: questions addressed to named people, responsive turns
common_mistakes: Trying to stay in second circle permanently
Confusing loudness with presence
drill: After each meeting this week, note which circle you spent most time in; the coach adds talk_share and question data.

sources.where: The Second Circle / Presence: three circles of energy

name: Open with a question about them
summary: Asking about the other person's priorities or situation, and following up on the answer, increases how much they like you. People underestimate this effect.
how_to_apply: Open 1:1s with a genuine question about their world, then ask one follow-up before turning to your agenda.
example_line: How did the board session go for you? What surprised you?
markers: questions by Tom in the first two minutes
Follow-up question referencing their answer
Their first-turn length (longer is better)
common_mistakes: Formulaic 'how are you?' with no follow-up
Interrogating instead of conversing
drill: Open every 1:1 this week with a question about them plus one follow-up. The coach counts.

sources.where: Huang et al. 2017: question-asking increases liking

name: Acknowledge the cost to them
summary: Recognising the burden or constraint your message places on someone ('I know this lands on your team') signals receptiveness and makes the message easier to accept.
how_to_apply: Before or after a demanding ask, name its specific cost to the listener in one sentence.
example_line: I know this means your team re-does the forecast, and I'm sorry about the timing.
markers: Acknowledgement phrases tied to the other person's constraint
Other speaker's tone and turn length after the ask
common_mistakes: Acknowledgement followed by 'but' that cancels it
Over-apologising
drill: For each request you make this week, add one sentence acknowledging its cost to the person.

sources.where: Yeomans et al. 2020: acknowledgement as receptiveness

name: Mirror their key words
summary: Repeating the last few words or the key phrase someone used encourages them to keep talking and signals that you are tracking. Mimicry in negotiation research improved outcomes.
how_to_apply: When someone says something important, repeat their key two or three words with a slight upward inflection, then wait.
example_line: Them: 'The handover was chaotic.' Tom: 'Chaotic?'
markers: Repetition of the other speaker's last words at the start of Tom's turn
The other person's next turn length (longer is the intended effect)
common_mistakes: Parroting constantly
Using it to extract information under false pretences
Mirroring tone when the other person is angry
drill: Use one mirror in each of three 1:1s this week and note whether the other person expanded.

sources.where: Maddux et al. 2008: mimicry in negotiation

ethics_note: Use to understand, not to manipulate. Mirroring to draw out information the other person would not knowingly share crosses into manipulation, especially with juniors.

name: Smile in the voice
summary: Warmth is audible: a slight smile changes the voice's tone, and listeners on calls hear it. It is one of the simplest warmth cues when there are no visual signals.
how_to_apply: On greetings, thanks and requests, let a genuine smile shape your voice; keep it for moments that warrant it.
example_line: (smiling) Great to hear from you. How's the new role?
markers: Not reliably measurable; pitch_sd_st slightly up and laughter around greetings are weak proxies
common_mistakes: Smiling through bad news
A fixed smile that sounds forced
drill: Record a voicemail-style greeting twice, with and without a smile, and listen back.

name: Small, relevant self-disclosure
summary: Sharing a small, relevant personal experience or uncertainty makes you more relatable and authentic, which recent executive surveys weight more than they used to.
how_to_apply: Occasionally share a brief, relevant personal angle (a lesson, a past mistake), then return to the topic.
example_line: I made exactly this hire mistake in my first company, so I'm wary of it.
markers: Brief first-person experience statements (one or two sentences)
Others reciprocating with their own experience
common_mistakes: Oversharing
Making the conversation about you
Disclosing to manipulate trust
drill: Plan one relevant disclosure for your next mentoring 1:1 and keep it under 30 seconds.

name: Remember and refer back
summary: Referring back to something personal or professional the other person mentioned before (a project, a family event) shows they matter to you.
how_to_apply: Note one thing from each 1:1 and open the next one by asking about it.
example_line: Last time you were dreading the audit. How did it go?
markers: References to prior conversations in the opening of 1:1s
common_mistakes: Using notes so obviously it feels like a CRM
Referring to private details in group settings
drill: Keep a one-line note after each 1:1 for a month and use it in the next one.

sources.where: Charisma Myth: making people feel important

name: Two follow-ups before a view
summary: Follow-up questions are the strongest single listening signal and increase liking. Asking two before giving your view also gathers better information.
how_to_apply: In 1:1s and problem discussions, ask at least two questions that build on what the person just said before you offer an opinion.
example_line: You mentioned the team's stretched. Which part of the work would you drop first?
markers: questions by Tom that reference the other's previous turn
Others' turn length after Tom's questions
Number of follow-ups before Tom's first opinion turn
common_mistakes: Leading questions that are statements in disguise
Interrogation without any view
Interrupting the answer
drill: In each 1:1 this week, ask two follow-ups before giving a view. The coach counts them.

name: Play it back before responding
summary: Summarising what you heard before responding shows you listened and checks understanding; in disagreement it lowers heat and makes your reply more persuasive.
how_to_apply: Before your counterpoint, restate the other view in one sentence and check: 'Have I got that right?'
example_line: So your worry is that we'd lose the partner, not the cost. Have I got that right?
markers: Paraphrase phrases ('so what I'm hearing', 'if I've got this right')
Confirmation from the other speaker ('yes, exactly')
common_mistakes: Paraphrasing to set up a rebuttal in a mocking tone
Paraphrasing at length
Getting it wrong and not correcting
drill: Before any disagreement this week, restate the other view in one sentence first. The coach counts paraphrases before counterpoints.

sources.where: Yeomans et al. 2020: acknowledging the other view

name: Talk the right share for the setting
summary: Command of the room is not airtime. In 1:1s with reports, talking less than half the time is usually right; in groups, fewer, higher-impact contributions carry more weight.
how_to_apply: Know your target band before you start (1:1 as manager ~30-50%; group participant ~1/N to 1.5/N), and check yourself at the halfway point.
example_line: (halfway) I've been talking a lot. Sam, what's your read?
markers: talk_share vs. rubric section 4 band for the setting
mean_turn_s and longest_turn_s (monologue risk above ~60-90 s in discussion)
common_mistakes: Going silent in senior rooms
Dominating because you know the material
Mechanically hitting a percentage
drill: For two weeks, the coach reports talk_share per setting; pick the setting furthest from its band and adjust.

name: Finish the sentence, then yield
summary: When interrupted on an important point, neither fight (louder, faster) nor fold (stop mid-point). Finish the current sentence at the same volume and pace, then hand over or signal you will return.
how_to_apply: Keep volume and pace steady, complete the sentence, then say 'let me finish this point, then I want your view' if needed.
example_line: ...which is why the date moves. Go ahead, then I'll come back to cost.
markers: interruptions of Tom and what follows (completion vs. abandonment)
loudness_db and speaking_rate_wpm during overlaps
Tom returning to the abandoned point later
common_mistakes: Raising volume to out-talk
Never returning to the dropped point
Using 'let me finish' aggressively
drill: With a colleague interrupting at random, practise finishing sentences at baseline volume. The coach checks loudness during overlaps.

sources.where: Hall et al. 2005: status and nonverbal cues

name: Invite the quiet person by name
summary: Drawing in someone who has not spoken, with a specific question, shows command of the room and widens the information you get.
how_to_apply: In each group meeting, name one person who has not spoken and ask a specific, answerable question.
example_line: Ana, you ran the last rollout. What would you watch out for?
markers: Names in Tom's questions to people with low talk_share so far
The invited person's turn length
common_mistakes: Putting someone on the spot with a hard question
Calling only on the same people
drill: In every group meeting this week, invite one quiet person by name. The coach checks who spoke after.

name: Do not interrupt to agree
summary: Supportive interruptions ('yes, exactly, and also...') still take the floor and can read as dominance or impatience. Let people land their point.
how_to_apply: When you agree, wait for the end of the sentence, then build: 'Building on that...'
example_line: (after Sam finishes) Building on Sam's point: the same applies to Leeds.
markers: interruptions by Tom with new content starting >0.3 s before the other ended
Supportive back-channels ('mm', 'yes') are fine and should not count
common_mistakes: Silence so complete it reads as disengagement
Saving up five points and delivering them at once
drill: The coach lists your competitive interruptions for a week; aim to halve them the next week.

name: Ask, then wait
summary: After asking a real question, the silence that follows is where the good answer forms. Filling it, rephrasing or answering it yourself kills it.
how_to_apply: Ask your question once, then count silently to five before saying anything else.
example_line: What's the one thing we're not saying? [waits]
markers: Gap after Tom's question before anyone speaks
Tom re-speaking within ~2 s of his own question (negative)
Stacked questions in one turn
common_mistakes: Rephrasing the question three times
Answering your own question
Waiting so long it becomes a power play
drill: In two meetings, after each open question, count to five silently. The coach measures the gaps.

sources.where: Think Faster, Talk Smarter: listening and pauses

name: One question at a time
summary: Stacking several questions in one turn lets the other person pick the easiest and signals nervousness. One clear, open question commands more.
how_to_apply: Ask a single open question ('what', 'how') and stop.
example_line: (not 'Is it the budget, or the team, or timing, or...?') What's really holding it up?
markers: Multiple question marks in one Tom turn
Closed vs. open question openers
common_mistakes: Closed questions when you want information
Leading questions
drill: For a week, the coach flags every stacked question; rewrite two of them as single open questions.

name: Check in when the signals change
summary: Presence includes noticing when the room has shifted (confusion, disagreement, low energy) and adjusting out loud rather than ploughing on.
how_to_apply: When you sense a shift, name it briefly and change approach: shorter, a different example, or a question.
example_line: I'm seeing some puzzled looks. Let me come at this differently.
markers: Others' clarifying questions or silence after Tom's turns
Tom's adjustment phrases ('let me put it another way', 'let me pause there')
Drop in back-channels during Tom's long turns
common_mistakes: Checking in so often it signals insecurity
Asking 'does that make sense?' as a reflex
drill: In your next presentation, plan two checkpoints where you read the room and adjust if needed.

name: Receive and appreciate while listening
summary: Small audible signals that you are taking it in ('mm', 'right') keep the speaker going and show presence, especially on calls where nods are invisible.
how_to_apply: On calls, use brief back-channels at natural pauses; do not take the floor with them.
example_line: Mm. Right. [lets them continue]
markers: Short back-channel tokens from Tom during others' turns (supportive overlaps)
Should not be counted as competitive interruptions
common_mistakes: Over-frequent 'yeah yeah yeah' that sounds impatient
Back-channels that turn into interruptions
drill: On your next three calls, use back-channels deliberately and ask the other person afterwards if you seemed engaged.

name: Synthesise where the room has got to
summary: Pulling a scattered discussion together ('So far we agree on A and B; C is open') is a high-presence move: it shows you were tracking everyone and helps the group move.
how_to_apply: When discussion loops, summarise in one or two sentences what is agreed and what remains open.
example_line: So we agree on the date and the budget; the open question is who leads. Let's settle that.
markers: Summary phrases ('so far', 'where we've got to', 'parking that') in group meetings
Discussion moving to a new topic after the summary
common_mistakes: Summarising in a way that misrepresents others
Summarising too early
drill: In each group meeting this week, offer one synthesis when the discussion loops.

name: Listen for the question behind the question
summary: Many questions carry an unstated concern (a cost question is often about risk or credibility). Answering the real concern shows depth and command.
how_to_apply: Before answering, ask yourself what the person is really worried about; answer the literal question briefly, then the underlying one.
example_line: The short answer is £40k. I suspect the real question is whether it pays back; it does, within a year.
markers: Tom's answers addressing both literal and underlying concerns
Questioner's follow-ups (fewer repeated questions is better)
common_mistakes: Guessing wrong and lecturing
Skipping the literal answer
drill: After your next Q&A, list each question and the concern behind it; check whether you addressed both.

name: Command through calm, not volume
summary: In a noisy or heated room, dropping your volume slightly and slowing down often draws attention better than raising your voice.
how_to_apply: When the room is loud or scattered, pause, then speak a little quieter and slower to bring people in.
example_line: (quiet, slow) Let's take a breath. Here's where we are.
markers: loudness_db and speaking_rate_wpm on Tom's turns in heated segments
Others' loudness after Tom's turn (falling is good)
common_mistakes: Going so quiet people cannot hear on a call
Sounding patronising
drill: In the next heated discussion, try one deliberately quieter intervention and note the effect.

name: Acknowledge, answer, add
summary: Respond to challenge in three beats: acknowledge the point in one sentence, answer directly (yes, no, a number), add the reason or next step. Receptive replies are rated better and persuade more.
how_to_apply: Practise the three beats until automatic; keep the acknowledgement genuine and short.
example_line: Fair challenge. Yes, we're over budget by 8%. Here's what we're doing about it.
markers: First sentence of reply: acknowledgement; second: direct answer word or number
Defensive markers absent ('to be fair', 'as I said')
Challenger's next turn shorter and calmer
common_mistakes: Acknowledging at length (sounds like stalling)
Acknowledging then contradicting with 'but'
Skipping the direct answer
drill: Have a colleague fire ten tough questions; answer each with acknowledge-answer-add. The coach scores first sentences.

name: Answer, detail, describe value
summary: A Q&A structure: give the answer, support it with one specific example, then say why it matters to the person who asked.
how_to_apply: Use it for questions after presentations and from senior stakeholders; adjust order if a quick example is needed first.
