example_line: Yes, it scales. We ran it with 40,000 users in Manchester. That means your region could go live in Q2.
markers: Direct answer in first sentence of Q&A replies
A concrete example in the reply
A relevance sentence addressed to the questioner
common_mistakes: Long details before the answer
Generic 'value' statements
drill: Prepare five likely questions for your next presentation and draft ADD answers under 30 seconds each.

name: Neutralise the loaded question
summary: Paraphrasing a hostile or loaded question into neutral terms before answering buys time, shows you listened, and stops you repeating the hostile framing.
how_to_apply: Restate the core of the question without its loaded words, then answer the neutral version.
example_line: Them: 'Why did you waste a year on this?' Tom: 'You're asking whether the year was worth it. Here's what it bought us.'
markers: Paraphrase of the question at the start of Tom's reply
Absence of the questioner's negative words in Tom's reply
common_mistakes: Paraphrasing into a different question (dodging)
Sounding like a politician
drill: Write five hostile questions you might face and practise a neutral paraphrase for each.

sources.where: media training: do not repeat the negative

name: Answer, then bridge
summary: Bridging moves from the question to your key message ('what matters most here is...'). Done after a genuine answer, it keeps a conversation on track; done instead of an answer, it reads as evasion.
how_to_apply: Give a short real answer first, then use a bridging phrase to link to your key message.
example_line: No, we didn't hit the target. What matters more is why, and what's changed since.
markers: Direct answer present before bridge phrases ('what matters most', 'the bigger point')
Questioner re-asking the same question (negative: dodge detected)
common_mistakes: Bridging without answering
Using the same bridge phrase repeatedly
Bridging in internal meetings where it sounds like spin
drill: In a mock Q&A, answer every question in one sentence before bridging. The coach checks for an answer before each bridge.
ethics_note: Bridging is legitimate only after a real answer. Used to avoid answering, it misleads listeners and erodes trust once noticed.

name: Answering a different question (recognise, do not use)
summary: Speakers can answer a similar but different question fluently, and listeners often fail to notice; detection rises sharply when the question is visible. It works in the moment and damages trust when caught.
how_to_apply: The coach should flag this in Tom's own replies so he can answer the real question instead. Not to be practised.
example_line: (dodge to avoid) Q: 'Did the launch slip?' A: 'Our launches are always rigorous...'
markers: Reply lacks the key term or answer type the question asked for (yes/no, number, date)
Questioner re-asks or narrows the question
common_mistakes: Thinking a fluent dodge is a win
Dodging in written follow-ups where the question is visible
drill: Review three tough questions from recent recordings: did each reply contain the answer type asked for? Rewrite any dodge as a direct answer.
ethics_note: Included so the coach can detect and discourage it. Deliberately answering a different question to mislead is manipulative; the coach must never recommend it.

name: Label the heat
summary: When a challenger is angry or anxious, naming the emotion calmly ('it sounds like this has caused real problems for your team') often lowers the temperature faster than arguing facts.
how_to_apply: Label first, pause, then address the substance. Use a calm, slower register.
example_line: It sounds like this has landed badly for your team. Tell me what's hit hardest.
markers: Label phrases at the start of replies to heated turns
Challenger's loudness_db and turn length after the label
common_mistakes: Labelling in a patronising tone
Using a label to avoid the substance
drill: Role-play two angry-stakeholder scenarios with a colleague, opening each reply with a label.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference: labelling negatives

name: Name their objections before they do
summary: Before a tough message, list the criticisms the other side is likely to have and voice them first. It takes the sting out and often prompts them to soften.
how_to_apply: Open a hard conversation with two or three of the likely objections, stated fairly and without exaggeration.
example_line: You're probably thinking this is another reorganisation dressed up, and that it'll land on your team again.
markers: Opening lines naming the listener's likely objections
The other side's reply tone (softer, 'it's not that bad')
common_mistakes: Exaggerating objections to provoke reassurance
Listing so many it becomes self-flagellation
drill: Before the next difficult message, write the three things they'll think, and open with them.

sources.where: Never Split the Difference: accusation audit

ethics_note: Only voice objections you genuinely believe they may hold. Exaggerating them to fish for reassurance is manipulative.

name: Concede the valid point quickly
summary: Agreeing fast with the part of a challenge that is right builds credibility for the part you dispute. Emphasising agreement is part of conversational receptiveness.
how_to_apply: Find what is correct in the challenge, agree with it explicitly, then state where you differ.
example_line: You're right that we under-forecast churn. Where I'd differ is on the cause.
markers: 'You're right that / I agree that' phrases in replies to challenge
Followed by a clearly marked difference ('where I see it differently')
common_mistakes: Conceding too much and losing the point
Fake concessions
drill: In the next three disagreements, start with a genuine concession. The coach counts receptiveness markers.

name: Disagree with receptive language
summary: Phrases that acknowledge the other view, state your claim as your view, and frame positively make disagreements more productive and persuasive, and others notice it even when the speaker doesn't.
how_to_apply: Use 'I see why you'd say that', 'From my view...', 'Where I see it differently is...' instead of 'That's wrong' or 'To be fair...'.
example_line: I see why you'd want to wait. From where I sit, waiting costs more.
markers: Receptiveness markers vs. defensive markers in challenge turns
Challenger's next turn calmer and shorter
common_mistakes: Using the phrases as a formula with a hostile tone
Contradicting the acknowledgement with 'but'
drill: The coach lists your defensive phrases from last week; replace each with a receptive equivalent in practice.

sources.where: Radical Candor: care personally, challenge directly

name: "I don't know" plus a plan
summary: Admitting you don't know, with a specific plan to find out, preserves credibility; bluffing and being found out costs far more.
how_to_apply: Say 'I don't know' plainly, then what you'll do and by when. Optionally share your best estimate, labelled as such.
example_line: I don't know the exact figure. My estimate is around 15%; I'll confirm by Thursday.
markers: Plain 'I don't know' + commitment phrases
Rambling or vague answers when the answer is unknown (negative)
common_mistakes: Over-apologising for not knowing
Saying 'I don't know' to things you should know
Never following up
drill: In a practice Q&A, include three questions you can't answer; use the not-knowing pattern each time.

name: Treat Q&A as conversation, not combat
summary: Framing tough questions as a dialogue with someone curious, rather than an attack, changes your voice and posture and reduces defensiveness.
how_to_apply: Before Q&A, remind yourself that questions mean engagement; respond as you would to a curious colleague.
example_line: Good question; it's the one I'd ask too.
markers: Defensive markers in Q&A replies
pitch_median_hz and speaking_rate_wpm stability in Q&A vs. presentation
common_mistakes: Praising every question ('great question') as a tic
Treating hostile questions as friendly when they are not
drill: Before your next Q&A, write one line reframing it as a conversation; compare Q&A stress markers afterwards.

name: Lower and slow under fire
summary: Under attack, the natural stress response pushes pitch up and pace faster. Deliberately keeping pace slower and pitch settled signals composure and helps you think.
how_to_apply: When challenged, slow your first sentence and keep pitch at baseline; take a breath before answering.
example_line: (slow, settled) Let me answer that directly.
markers: pitch_median_hz rise > ~1-2 st and speaking_rate_wpm rise > ~15-20% on challenged turns (rubric heuristics)
pitch_sd_st collapse
common_mistakes: Slowing so much it sounds patronising
Going monotone
drill: Record replies to five challenging questions and compare pitch and rate with baseline; repeat until within your normal range.

sources.where: Cheng et al. 2016: pitch and rank

name: Dare to be dull: aim for good enough
summary: When put on the spot, trying to be brilliant creates freeze. Aiming for a clear, adequate answer reduces pressure and usually produces a better one.
how_to_apply: When called on unexpectedly, give a plain, structured answer; drop the aim of being impressive.
example_line: Honest answer: I'd want more data, but my instinct is yes, for two reasons.
markers: Fillers and restarts in unplanned turns vs. planned ones
Length of impromptu turns (short is fine)
common_mistakes: Using 'good enough' as an excuse not to prepare for predictable questions
drill: Ask a colleague to spring three questions on you during the week; answer each plainly in under 30 seconds.

name: Buy time honestly
summary: Saying you need a moment, or restating the question, gives you a few seconds to structure your answer without sounding caught out.
how_to_apply: Use a short honest buffer ('Let me think about that for a second') or a paraphrase, then answer with a structure.
example_line: Let me take a second on that. [pause] Two things.
markers: median_response_gap_s on unexpected questions
Buffer phrase followed by structured answer (vs. fillers)
common_mistakes: Using buffers every time
Taking 'a second' and then rambling
drill: Practise five unexpected questions using a buffer and a two-point structure.

name: Prepare a message house
summary: Before a high-stakes meeting or interview, prepare one headline message and three supporting pillars with evidence. Under pressure you return to the house instead of improvising.
how_to_apply: Write the headline (roof) and three pillars with one proof each on a single card; return to them when answering.
example_line: (headline) We're profitable next year. (pillars) Costs down, prices up, churn falling.
markers: Recurrence of the headline and pillars across Tom's answers
Consistency of message across the meeting
common_mistakes: Repeating the message robotically regardless of the question
Pillars without evidence
drill: Build a message house for your next board or investor meeting and rehearse answering five questions from it.

name: Lead with a weakness before the strengths
summary: Mentioning a genuine drawback early (and then your strongest points) makes you come across as more honest and makes the strengths more believable.
how_to_apply: When presenting a proposal, name its main real limitation briefly, then the strengths that outweigh it.
example_line: It's not the cheapest option. It is the only one we can deliver by June.
markers: Early mention of a limitation followed by strengths in proposal turns
common_mistakes: Dwelling on the weakness
Inventing a trivial weakness as a ploy
drill: Rewrite your next proposal opening so it names one real limitation in the first two sentences.

name: One idea in fifteen words
summary: Every talk or contribution should carry one main idea you can state in a single short sentence. If you cannot, the message is not ready.
how_to_apply: Write the throughline in 15 words or fewer before any important meeting; everything you say should serve it.
example_line: We should stop building features and fix onboarding first.
markers: Recurrence of a single headline across Tom's turns
Number of distinct claims per substantive turn (fewer is better)
common_mistakes: A throughline so general it says nothing
Cramming in every point you know
drill: Before your next three key meetings, write your throughline in 15 words; afterwards, ask one attendee what your point was.

name: Halve it
summary: Most answers are better at half the length. Senior listeners reward economy; length often reads as uncertainty or lack of preparation.
how_to_apply: Re-record or rewrite your answer at half the length, keeping the headline and the strongest reason.
example_line: (two-minute answer cut to one) Yes. It pays back in a year, and the risk is low.
markers: mean_turn_s and longest_turn_s in senior settings vs. baseline
Word count of answers to direct questions
common_mistakes: Cutting the reason and leaving only the claim
Speaking faster instead of saying less
drill: Pick your longest answer from last week's transcript and re-record it at half the length; the coach compares word counts.

name: Thirty-second answers upward
summary: With senior stakeholders, aim to answer most questions in about thirty seconds, then offer more detail if wanted. It shows command and respects their time.
how_to_apply: Answer, give one reason, then stop and offer: 'Want the detail?'
example_line: We're on track for June. The one risk is supplier capacity. Happy to go deeper.
markers: Duration of Tom's answers to questions from senior speakers (target ~30-45 s)
longest_turn_s in board or investor recordings
common_mistakes: Cutting so short you sound evasive
Offering detail and then giving it anyway
drill: Practise ten likely senior questions with a timer; aim for 30 seconds each.

name: Attach the so-what to every fact
summary: Facts without implications make the listener do the work. Executives want to know what a number means for them.
how_to_apply: After each fact, add 'which means...' or 'so...' in the listener's terms.
example_line: Churn rose to 4%, which means we lose a month of growth every quarter.
markers: Facts followed by implication phrases ('which means', 'so', 'the implication is')
Others asking 'so what does that mean?' (negative)
common_mistakes: Implications that overreach the data
Explaining obvious implications to experts
drill: Review a recent update; add a 'which means' after each number and present the revised version.

name: Lead with the ask
summary: When you need something (a decision, money, help), say so at the start. Burying the ask after context makes listeners wonder what the meeting is for.
how_to_apply: Open with what you need and by when; then give the reasons.
example_line: I need a yes on two contractors today. Here's why.
markers: Explicit ask phrases ('I need', 'I'm asking for', 'the decision I'd like') in the first minute
Others asking 'what do you need from us?' (negative)
common_mistakes: Asking without context at all
Asking for several things at once
drill: For every meeting you request this week, put the ask in the first sentence. The coach checks first-minute asks.

name: Skip the backstory
summary: Chronological backstory before the point is the most common cause of long, unclear contributions. Context should come only as needed to support the conclusion.
how_to_apply: Start with the conclusion; add backstory only if asked or if one fact is essential.
example_line: (not 'So back in March, we started...') The vendor failed. Here's what we're doing.
markers: Time words ('back in', 'initially', 'then') dominating the first half of a turn
Claim position late in the turn
common_mistakes: Removing context the listener genuinely needs
Over-terse answers to newcomers
drill: The coach flags your three longest chronological openings this week; re-record each starting from the conclusion.

name: Make one number meaningful
summary: One well-chosen number, put into context (a comparison or a picture), lands better than a slide of figures.
how_to_apply: Choose the one number that matters and compare it to something familiar.
example_line: We lose 400 customers a month. That's a full branch, every month.
markers: Count of numbers per turn (fewer, contextualised)
Comparison phrases attached to numbers
common_mistakes: Comparisons that distort scale
A string of unexplained figures
drill: For your next update, pick one number and write a comparison for it.

name: Three headlines before the meeting
summary: Writing down the two or three things you most want to say before a meeting means you say them early and crisply rather than discovering them mid-sentence.
how_to_apply: Before the meeting, write up to three one-sentence headlines; make sure each gets said.
example_line: (card) 1: Delay launch. 2: Fund testing. 3: I'll brief the partner.
markers: Prepared headlines appearing verbatim or near-verbatim in the transcript
Position of the first headline in Tom's first substantive turn
common_mistakes: Forcing headlines in regardless of the discussion
Having too many
drill: Before five meetings this week, write three headlines. The coach checks how many were said and when.

name: Stop when you're done
summary: Adding 'just one more thing' or repeating a point in different words dilutes the message and signals uncertainty that it landed.
how_to_apply: When you have made your point, stop. If you have one more genuinely new point, signal it ('one final, separate point').
example_line: That's the recommendation. [stop]
markers: Restatements of the same point within one turn
Add-on phrases ('just to add', 'also, one more thing') at the end of turns
common_mistakes: Stopping before making the point at all
drill: The coach flags every repeated point within a turn for a week; aim to cut them by half.

name: Status, risk, ask
summary: A three-part update for senior audiences: where we are, the main risk, and what you need. It replaces long progress narratives.
how_to_apply: Structure updates as one sentence each for status, risk and ask.
example_line: Status: on track for June. Risk: supplier capacity. Ask: approve a backup supplier.
markers: All three parts present in update turns
Update turn length under ~60 s
common_mistakes: Hiding the risk
No ask when one is needed
drill: Deliver your next three updates in status-risk-ask form and time them.

name: Strip jargon and acronyms
summary: Jargon and internal acronyms make you sound like you are hiding behind language and lose people outside your team. Plain words sound more senior, not less.
how_to_apply: Replace acronyms and buzzwords with plain words, or define them once.
example_line: (not 'leverage our GTM synergies') Sell both products through the same sales team.
markers: Acronym and buzzword density in the transcript
Others asking what a term means
common_mistakes: Over-explaining terms experts know
drill: The coach lists your top five jargon terms of the week; find a plain replacement for each.

name: Time-box presentations well under the slot
summary: Shorter presentations hold attention and leave room for discussion; TED caps talks at 18 minutes for this reason. For internal slots, aim to use about half the time to present.
how_to_apply: Plan to finish presenting at roughly half the allotted time, leaving the rest for questions and decision.
example_line: I'll take ten minutes, then I'd like twenty on the decision.
markers: Duration of Tom's presentation segment vs. meeting slot
longest_turn_s in presentation recordings
common_mistakes: Rushing to fit too much into less time
Cutting the structure instead of content
drill: Rehearse your next presentation with a timer set to half the slot.

name: Bad news early, with a plan
summary: Raising bad news early and plainly, with a recommendation attached, is a mark of gravitas; executives list speaking truth to power among presence traits.
how_to_apply: Put the bad news in the first sentence or two, state its size plainly, then your recommended response.
example_line: We're going to miss Q3 by about 10%. Here's what I recommend we do.
markers: Position of bad news in the turn (early is better)
hedges_per_100w and apologies in bad-news turns vs. baseline
Recommendation following the bad news
common_mistakes: Burying bad news after good news
Over-apologising
Bad news with no plan
drill: For your next difficult update upward, write the first two sentences in advance: the news and the recommendation.

name: Same voice up as across
summary: Presence with a board or investors means sounding like you do with peers: same pace, pitch and directness. The usual tell is pitch and pace rising and hedges increasing when speaking up.
how_to_apply: Before senior meetings, remind yourself to speak as a colleague; compare your recordings across settings.
example_line: (to the chair, at peer pace) I disagree, and here's why.
markers: Deltas in pitch_median_hz, speaking_rate_wpm, hedges_per_100w and uptalk_share between senior and peer meetings
apologies in upward settings
common_mistakes: Overcorrecting into overfamiliarity
Mimicking senior people's style
drill: The coach produces a side-by-side of your voice and hedge measures in senior vs. peer meetings; pick the biggest gap to close.

name: Play high or low on purpose
summary: Gruenfeld (drawing on theatre) describes 'playing high' (authority: fewer words, direct statements, unhurried delivery) and 'playing low' (approachability: questions, deference, warmth). Effective leaders choose deliberately.
how_to_apply: Before a meeting, decide which you need: high with a sceptical board under challenge, lower with a junior team you want ideas from.
example_line: (playing high) We'll proceed. (playing low) What am I missing?
markers: Ratio of questions to statements by setting
talk_share and interruptions by setting
Hedges and apologies when playing high (should be low)
common_mistakes: Playing high with juniors who need safety
Playing low with a board that needs a decision
Staying in one mode always
drill: For one week, label each meeting 'high' or 'low' in advance; the coach checks the questions-to-statements ratio against your label.

name: Enter by building on the last speaker
summary: In fast senior discussions, the cleanest way in is to connect to what was just said, then add your point. It earns the floor without fighting for it.
how_to_apply: Use the previous speaker's name and point as your bridge, then make your contribution in one or two sentences.
example_line: Building on Claire's point about cost: there's a timing risk too.
markers: Name + 'building on / to Claire's point' openings
Time to Tom's first contribution in group meetings
common_mistakes: Waiting for a perfect gap that never comes
Building on someone just to repeat them
drill: In three group meetings, make your first contribution within the first ten minutes using a build. The coach checks timing.

name: Open with substance, not deference
summary: Openers like 'sorry, if I may, just a quick thought' signal low status before the content arrives. A direct, polite entry carries more weight.
how_to_apply: Start with the person's name or a short bridge, then the point.
example_line: (not 'Sorry, if I could just...') Chair, one point on risk.
markers: apologies and minimisers in the first five words of Tom's contributions in senior settings
common_mistakes: Sounding curt
Interrupting rather than waiting for a gap
drill: For one week, the coach flags every deferential opener in upward meetings; replace each with a name-plus-point opener.

name: Disagree upward with respect and reason
summary: Disagreeing with seniors works best when you acknowledge their view, state yours as your judgement, and give a reason. Receptive disagreement is persuasive without being insubordinate.
how_to_apply: Use: 'I understand why you'd go that way. My concern is X, because Y. I'd suggest Z.'
example_line: I see why you'd want to move fast. My concern is the contract, because it isn't signed. I'd wait two weeks.
markers: Receptive markers + first-person judgement + reason in disagreement turns with seniors
Hedges and permission tags in those turns (negative)
common_mistakes: Disagreeing only in private afterwards
Over-softening so the disagreement is missed
drill: Prepare one respectful disagreement for your next senior meeting using the pattern.

name: Frame for their agenda
summary: Senior people listen for what matters to them. Framing your point in terms of their priorities shows strategic awareness and earns attention.
how_to_apply: Before the meeting, identify the senior person's top concern and link your headline to it.
example_line: Given your focus on cash this year, this frees up £2m by Q2.
markers: References to the listener's stated priorities in Tom's turns
Senior person's engagement (questions, follow-ups)
common_mistakes: Pandering
Guessing their priorities wrongly
drill: Before your next senior meeting, write their top priority and connect your headline to it.

name: Ask the sharp question
summary: In senior rooms, a precise, curious question often carries more presence than a statement. Influence earned through expertise and curiosity is respected and liked.
how_to_apply: Prepare one incisive question that shows you've understood the core issue; ask it calmly.
example_line: What would have to be true for this to pay back in a year?
markers: Tom's questions in senior meetings and the responses they trigger
Others picking up or repeating Tom's question
common_mistakes: Gotcha questions
Questions to show off
drill: For each senior meeting this month, prepare one sharp question.

name: Spell out the bottom line for direct cultures
summary: British indirectness can be read as weakness or missed entirely by Dutch, German or many US colleagues. With these audiences, state the conclusion and its severity explicitly.
how_to_apply: In international meetings, say the bottom line explicitly and avoid understatement on key points.
example_line: To be clear: this is a serious problem and we should stop.
markers: Downgraders on serious issues in mixed-culture meetings
Clarifying questions from international colleagues
common_mistakes: Overcorrecting with UK colleagues
Assuming nationality defines style
drill: Before your next international call, rewrite your key point without understatement.

name: Drop the over-deference
summary: Excessive thanks, honorifics or 'if I may' in senior rooms signal that you see yourself as junior. Courtesy is good; deference is a status tell.
how_to_apply: Thank once, use names rather than titles where culturally appropriate, and drop 'if I may' and 'with respect'.
example_line: Thanks, James. Here's what I'd suggest.
markers: Count of deferential phrases ('if I may', 'with respect', 'sorry to take up time') in upward settings vs. peer settings
apologies
common_mistakes: Becoming over-familiar
Ignoring cultural norms where titles matter
drill: The coach counts deferential phrases in your next three senior meetings; cut them by half.

name: Have the one-minute version ready
summary: Senior slots get cut. Having a one-minute version of your message ready means you hold your ground when time shrinks instead of rushing a ten-minute version.
how_to_apply: Prepare a 60-second version of every important presentation; if your time is cut, switch to it calmly.
example_line: We've only got two minutes, so here's the one-minute version.
markers: speaking_rate_wpm spikes when time is cut (rushing, negative)
Clean shortened structure after a time cut
common_mistakes: Speeding through the full deck
Complaining about the time cut
drill: For your next presentation, rehearse the one-minute version twice.

name: Prestige, not dominance
summary: There are two routes to influence: dominance (interrupting, pressure) and prestige (sharing expertise, generosity). Both work, but only prestige is liked and sustains respect.
how_to_apply: Influence by teaching and sharing know-how freely; avoid floor-grabbing, sarcasm and pressure tactics.
example_line: Happy to share how we did this at the last company; it might save you a month.
markers: interruptions by Tom and sarcasm (dominance cues)
Offers to share expertise or help (prestige cues)
Others asking Tom for his view (prestige outcome)
common_mistakes: Lecturing (prestige tipping into dominance)
False modesty
drill: The coach tallies dominance and prestige cues across a month; review the balance.

name: Keep your pitch level when presenting up
summary: Status nerves show up in the voice: pitch and rate rise when speaking to seniors. Keeping them near your baseline makes you sound like you belong in the room.
how_to_apply: Before speaking up, breathe out, find your relaxed pitch, and slow the first sentence slightly.
example_line: (settled) Thanks. Three points from me.
markers: pitch_median_hz and speaking_rate_wpm in upward settings vs. peer baseline
pitch_drift_st across the senior meeting
common_mistakes: Forcing a low voice
Over-slowing
drill: Record your next two board or investor sessions; the coach compares pitch and rate with peer-meeting baseline.
